props.title: Pride and Prejudice and Zombies
props.initialSlug: Jane Austen meets zombie apocalypse in England

sections.content: **Pride and Prejudice and Zombies (2016)** (2016) exemplifies the literary mashup trend that exploded after Seth Grahame-Smith's 2009 novel. The film blends Jane Austen's marriage plot with zombie horror, following the Bennet sisters as both accomplished warriors and marriage-minded ladies. This spawned similar genre hybrids like Abraham Lincoln: Vampire Hunter (2012) and influenced meta-horror comedies like **The Final Girls** (2015). While the execution is uneven, it demonstrates horror's ability to infiltrate classic literature.

sections.content: The film sits within a larger trend of reimagining classic works through genre lenses. **Anna and the Apocalypse** (2017) turned the high school musical into a Christmas zombie fest, while **Hansel & Gretel: Witch Hunters** (2013) gave the fairy tale an R-rated action makeover. These adaptations reflect our desire to make historical works relevant through modern genre conventions, though they often struggle to balance reverence for the source material with their wilder genre elements.

The combat sequences in **Pride and Prejudice and Zombies** draw from both period martial arts films like **House of Flying Daggers** (2004) and modern zombie action like **World War Z** (2013). The Bennet sisters' fighting styles incorporate proper Regency-era ladylike movements with deadly efficiency, creating a unique aesthetic that comments on female empowerment while maintaining period authenticity. sections.content: While George Romero established serious zombie commentary with **Night of the Living Dead** (1968), films like **Return of the Living Dead** (1985) proved zombies could fuel comedy. **Pride and Prejudice and Zombies** follows this tradition, using the undead for both scares and satirical purposes. The film's approach to class warfare - with upper-class zombie hunters trained in Japan while poor fighters learn in China - adds social commentary that both Austen and Romero would appreciate.
